# Git Rebase vs Git Merge

## What They Do

Both integrate changes from one branch into another, but they do it differently.

### Git Merge
Creates a **new merge commit** that ties together the histories of both branches.

```
Before:                    After merge:
                           
A---B---C  (main)          A---B---C---M  (main)
     \                          \     /
      D---E  (feature)           D---E
```
The history shows exactly what happened and when.

### Git Rebase
**Replays** your commits on top of another branch, rewriting history.

```
Before:                    After rebase:

A---B---C  (main)          A---B---C---D'---E'  (feature)
     \                                 
      D---E  (feature)     
```
Commits D and E become D' and E' — same changes, new commit hashes.

---

## When to Use Each

### Use Merge When:
- Merging a **completed feature into main/develop**
- You want to **preserve the true history** of what happened
- Working on a **shared/public branch** (never rebase these)
- You want a clear record of when branches were integrated

```bash
git checkout main
git merge feature/my-feature
```

### Use Rebase When:
- **Updating your local feature branch** with latest main changes
- You want a **clean, linear history** before merging
- Doing an **interactive rebase** to clean up messy commits
- Working on a **private branch** only you use

```bash
git checkout feature/my-feature
git rebase main
```

---

## Interactive Rebase — A Superpower

```bash
git rebase -i HEAD~4   # Rewrite last 4 commits
```

This lets you:
- `pick` — keep a commit as-is
- `squash` — combine with previous commit
- `reword` — edit the commit message
- `drop` — delete a commit entirely
- `edit` — pause to amend the commit

**Great for cleaning up "WIP", "fix typo", "oops" commits before merging.**

---

## The Tradeoffs

| | Merge | Rebase |
|---|---|---|
| History | Preserves exact history | Creates cleaner linear history |
| Commit hashes | Unchanged | Rewritten (new hashes) |
| Merge commit | Yes | No |
| Conflict resolution | Once, at merge time | Once per replayed commit |
| Safe on shared branches | ✅ Yes | ❌ No |
| Easier to understand | For some | For others |
| `git bisect` friendly | Somewhat | Very |

---

## The Golden Rule

> **Never rebase a branch that others are working on.**

When you rebase, you rewrite commit hashes. If someone else has those old commits, their history diverges from yours and you'll create a mess.

```bash
# DANGEROUS if anyone else has pulled feature-branch
git rebase main feature-branch   # ❌ if shared

# SAFE — only you use your local feature branch
git rebase main                   # ✅ on your private branch
```

---

## A Common Workflow

```bash
# 1. Keep your feature branch updated with main (rebase)
git checkout feature/my-feature
git fetch origin
git rebase origin/main

# 2. Clean up commits before merging (interactive rebase)
git rebase -i origin/main

# 3. Merge the clean branch into main
git checkout main
git merge --no-ff feature/my-feature  # --no-ff preserves merge commit
```

---

## Quick Decision Guide

```
Is the branch shared with others?
├── Yes → Use MERGE
└── No → 
    Do you want clean linear history?
    ├── Yes → REBASE, then merge
    └── No → MERGE is fine
```

The most common practical approach: **rebase locally to stay current, merge to integrate.**
